cn-4: Brainstem consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla; it links cerebrum, cerebellum, and spinal cord and contains cranial motor/sensory nuclei, long tracts, and autonomic networks.
Tectum is the dorsal midbrain roof behind the aqueduct; tegmentum is the central region; basis is the ventral region containing major descending fibers and, in pons, pontine nuclei.
Orient a section in sequence: level → dorsal/ventral → medial/lateral. A ventral peduncle/pyramid is not interchangeable with a dorsal sensory nucleus.
cn-5: Midbrain landmarks: ventral cerebral peduncles and dorsal superior/inferior colliculi. Superior colliculi participate in visual orienting; inferior colliculi in auditory processing/orienting.
Pons has a large ventral basilar portion and prominent middle cerebellar peduncles laterally; its dorsal surface contributes to the fourth ventricular floor.

Medulla shows ventral pyramids carrying corticospinal fibers and olives overlying inferior olivary nuclei. Dorsal caudal medulla includes gracile/cuneate tubercles and a central canal; rostral open medulla borders fourth ventricle.
The original anterior/posterior diagrams also show the aqueduct/ventricular region, cerebellar peduncles, and longitudinal surface grooves; use these to orient the complete retained images.
cn-6: CN III attaches ventrally to midbrain near the interpeduncular region; CN IV is unique in exiting dorsally below the inferior colliculus before wrapping around the brainstem.
CN V attaches to lateral pons. CN VI attaches near the midline pontomedullary junction; VII and VIII attach more laterally near the cerebellopontine angle.
CN IX and X emerge lateral to the medullary olive; XII emerges between pyramid and olive. Attachment location helps infer the level of a focal lesion.
Spinal CN XI rootlets arise from upper cervical cord, ascend through foramen magnum, then leave through jugular foramen. They are not simply another nucleus confined to medulla.
cn-7: Names in numerical order: I olfactory, II optic, III oculomotor, IV trochlear, V trigeminal, VI abducens, VII facial, VIII vestibulocochlear, IX glossopharyngeal, X vagus, XI accessory, XII hypoglossal.
Trigeminal divisions are V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary, and V3 mandibular. The slide's 'abducent' is an alternative form of abducens.
I and II are associated with forebrain rather than brainstem attachments; II is a CNS extension with oligodendrocyte myelin and meningeal coverings.
The anterior/posterior views locate roots relative to the peduncles, pons, medullary pyramid/olive, and cervical cord; identifying a root is different from identifying its deep nucleus.
cn-8: Internal carotid circulation gives ACA and MCA. Paired vertebral arteries supply PICA branches and unite to form basilar artery.
Basilar branches include pontine arteries, AICA, and SCA, then it terminates in paired PCAs. Variants are common, so these are the usual anatomical relationships.
Anterior communicating artery connects the ACAs; posterior communicating arteries link internal carotid circulation with PCAs.

The circle proper includes proximal ACA/PCA segments, communicating arteries, and terminal internal carotid connections; MCA and cerebellar arteries are adjacent branches rather than components of the ring.
cn-9: Midbrain is supplied by branches from PCA and SCA, with contributions varying by level and precise territory.
Pons is supplied by basilar paramedian/circumferential branches and contributions from AICA and SCA; medial and lateral territories differ.

Medulla is supplied by vertebral, PICA, and anterior spinal branches. Medial medulla classically involves ASA/paramedian vertebral supply; lateral medulla commonly involves vertebral or PICA territory.
An artery name alone does not specify every structure injured; combine vascular territory with the clinical and cross-sectional pattern.
cn-11: GSE/general somatic efferent supplies somite-related skeletal muscles: ocular motor III/IV/VI and tongue XII are major examples.

SVE/special visceral efferent is branchial motor to pharyngeal-arch-derived skeletal muscle, including mastication V3, facial expression VII, and stylopharyngeus/pharyngeal-laryngeal muscles IX/X. 'Visceral' here does not mean smooth muscle.
GVE/general visceral efferent is autonomic, here mainly preganglionic parasympathetic output in III, VII, IX, and X to glands, smooth muscle, and heart.

SVA/special visceral afferent carries smell and taste; GVA/general visceral afferent carries internal-organ and reflex sensory input; GSA/general somatic afferent carries general touch, pain, temperature, and related somatic sensation.
SSA/special somatic afferent carries vision, hearing, and balance. Efferent means away from CNS; afferent means toward CNS.
cn-12: Opening of the embryonic hindbrain into fourth ventricle spreads sensory alar-plate derivatives laterally; motor basal-plate derivatives remain more medial.
Sulcus limitans separates motor/efferent and sensory/afferent territories. The functional-column diagram is a developmental framework, not a rigid straight line through every adult nucleus.
GSE, branchial motor/SVE, and autonomic/GVE nuclei occupy motor territory; visceral/taste, somatic sensory, and vestibulocochlear nuclei occupy sensory territory.
Solitary nucleus receives both SVA taste, mainly rostrally, and GVA visceral input, mainly caudally. A shared nucleus does not make taste a GSA modality.
cn-13: Typical level map: III/IV → midbrain; V/VI/VII and much of VIII → pons/pontomedullary region; IX/X/XII → medulla; spinal XI → upper cervical cord.
Several sensory nuclei extend across levels: mesencephalic V reaches midbrain/rostral pons; spinal trigeminal descends through medulla into upper cervical cord; vestibular nuclei span pons/medulla.
The retained map includes oculomotor/EW, trochlear, trigeminal motor/sensory, abducens, facial, salivatory, vestibulocochlear, ambiguus, solitary, dorsal motor X, and hypoglossal nuclei.
The slide's study guidance is source content. These notes explain the complete map while emphasizing localization through level and function.
cn-15: LR6, SO4, all others III: lateral rectus receives VI; superior oblique receives IV; medial/superior/inferior recti and inferior oblique receive III.
CN III also innervates levator palpebrae superioris to elevate the upper lid. Orbicularis oculi closes the lid through VII and is a different muscle.
The diagram identifies recti around the globe, obliques, superior oblique tendon/trochlea, optic nerve, and common tendinous-ring region; nerve identity follows the muscle rather than its name alone.
cn-16: Anatomical action depends on the muscle's line of pull and the current eye position. Clinical testing positions the globe to preferentially isolate a vertical component.
Medial rectus adducts; lateral rectus abducts. Superior/inferior recti elevate/depress most selectively when the eye is abducted; obliques are tested for vertical movement with the eye adducted.
Superior rectus also intorts/adducts; inferior rectus also extorts/adducts; superior oblique also intorts/abducts; inferior oblique also extorts/abducts.
The phrase 'down and in' describes testing superior oblique with an adducted eye, not its full anatomical vector or a claim that superior oblique itself primarily adducts.
The original video link is retained in the extracted text; the written comparisons and images provide the study content without requiring that external video.
cn-17: Clinical H-pattern: medial rectus → adduct; lateral rectus → abduct; superior rectus → abduct then elevate; inferior rectus → abduct then depress.
Superior oblique → adduct then depress; inferior oblique → adduct then elevate. Compare the two eyes for restricted movement and diplopia.
Vertical recti are isolated in abduction, while obliques are isolated in adduction. These are exam positions rather than complete action lists.
cn-18: Oculomotor GSE neurons in midbrain supply most extraocular muscles and levator; Edinger-Westphal preganglionic GVE neurons provide ocular parasympathetic output.
CN III travels near the posterior communicating region, through cavernous sinus lateral wall, and enters the orbit through superior orbital fissure.
Parasympathetic route: Edinger-Westphal → III → ciliary ganglion synapse → short ciliary nerves → sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.
Sphincter contraction causes miosis; ciliary muscle contraction allows the lens to become rounder for near accommodation. These are separate from skeletal extraocular movement.
cn-19: A complete peripheral III palsy can cause ptosis, a down-and-out eye from relatively unopposed VI/IV actions, diplopia, impaired accommodation, and mydriasis if parasympathetic fibers are affected.
Compressive lesions such as a PCOM-region aneurysm often involve superficial pupilloconstrictor fibers; microvascular ischemia often relatively spares the pupil.

Pupil sparing is a tendency, not a reliable rule excluding an aneurysm or other compression. Acute painful/new III palsy requires appropriate urgent assessment rather than reassurance from the pupil alone.
The 3Ds aid recall of a typical complete palsy but incomplete lesions may lack one or more findings.
cn-20: Trochlear nucleus lies in caudal midbrain near inferior colliculus; axons decussate in the superior medullary velum and exit dorsally.
CN IV travels through cavernous sinus lateral wall and superior orbital fissure to superior oblique. Its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to trauma.
Superior oblique intorts the eye and depresses an adducted eye; testing 'down and in' isolates its depressive action.
A pre-crossing trochlear nuclear lesion weakens the contralateral superior oblique; a peripheral IV nerve lesion weakens the ipsilateral muscle.
cn-21: IV palsy produces vertical/torsional diplopia, especially when looking downward with the eye adducted, such as reading or descending stairs.
The affected eye can be relatively elevated and extorted. Patients often tilt the head away from the affected side to reduce misalignment.
Do not confuse head tilt away in IV palsy with head turn toward the affected side often used in VI palsy; compensatory postures depend on the alignment problem.
cn-22: Abducens nucleus lies in caudal pons; the nerve emerges near midline at the pontomedullary junction and innervates ipsilateral lateral rectus.
Its intracranial route includes a long course near the clivus/Dorello canal and cavernous sinus adjacent to the internal carotid before entering superior orbital fissure.

Peripheral VI output abducts one eye. The abducens nucleus also contains interneurons coordinating opposite medial rectus through the MLF, so a nuclear lesion can impair conjugate gaze rather than only one muscle.
cn-23: Peripheral VI palsy weakens lateral rectus: the affected eye cannot abduct fully and may rest medially in esotropia.
Horizontal diplopia worsens looking toward the affected side, and patients may turn the head toward that side to reduce required eye excursion.
Raised intracranial pressure can cause a VI palsy as a false-localizing sign; an isolated VI deficit does not always identify a pontine infarct.
cn-25: CN V attaches to pons and is the major somatic sensory nerve of face, cornea, oral/nasal regions, teeth, and much dura.
V1 and V2 are sensory; V3 contains somatic sensory and branchial motor components. Trigeminal ganglion contains most primary sensory somata; motor fibers bypass its sensory relay role.
V1 broadly supplies forehead/cornea/upper nose; V2 midface/upper teeth; V3 lower face/lower teeth and anterior tongue general sensation, with motor fibers to mastication.
The mandibular angle is an important regional exception, receiving upper cervical rather than typical trigeminal cutaneous supply.
cn-26: V1 exits through superior orbital fissure, V2 through foramen rotundum, and V3 through foramen ovale.
The original color map relates each division to face, nasal/oral mucosa, teeth, and skull foramina. Division and route are useful together when localizing skull-base injury.
CN III/IV/VI also traverse superior orbital fissure; CN II uses optic canal. A lesion of one opening can affect multiple structures rather than an entire cranial nerve category.
cn-27: Mesencephalic V mediates proprioceptive information from jaw-related structures; it unusually contains primary sensory neuron cell bodies inside the CNS.
Principal/chief trigeminal sensory nucleus in pons handles discriminative touch/vibration; spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract handles pain/temperature and extends caudally.
Second-order face sensory pathways ascend mainly to contralateral VPM thalamus; body somatosensation uses VPL. Some oral sensory projections are bilateral.
A lesion of the ipsilateral descending spinal V tract/nucleus before crossing can impair face pain-temperature while nearby spinothalamic injury impairs the opposite body.
cn-28: Trigeminal motor nucleus in pons sends SVE fibers through V3 to masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, and lateral pterygoid.
Masseter and temporalis strongly elevate the mandible; temporalis also retracts. Pterygoids contribute protrusion and side-to-side movements, with lateral pterygoid important in opening/protrusion.
A unilateral LMN motor V3 lesion weakens ipsilateral mastication; on opening, the intact side pushes the jaw toward the weak/lesioned side.
Other V3 branchial motor targets include mylohyoid, anterior digastric belly, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini; these help distinguish V3 from VII/X motor supply.
cn-29: Facial nerve attaches near pontomedullary junction and contains SVE to facial-expression muscles; GVE to lacrimal, submandibular/sublingual glands; SVA anterior tongue taste; and a small GSA external-ear component.
VII enters internal acoustic meatus with VIII, traverses facial canal, and exits stylomastoid foramen before branching within parotid gland.
Superior salivatory-related parasympathetic neurons feed VII pathways; geniculate ganglion contains sensory somata, not the parasympathetic synapse.
Passing through parotid does not mean VII supplies its secretomotor innervation: parotid parasympathetics originate in IX.
cn-30: Greater petrosal branches near geniculate region and conveys preganglionic parasympathetics toward pterygopalatine ganglion for lacrimal/nasal/palatal secretion.

Nerve to stapedius dampens stapes movement; injury can cause hyperacusis. Chorda tympani crosses middle ear and joins lingual V3, carrying anterior-tongue taste and preganglionic input to submandibular ganglion.
Submandibular ganglion supplies submandibular/sublingual glands; greater petrosal does not relay there. Extracranial VII branches primarily supply facial-expression muscles.
A proximal lesion can affect tears, taste, stapedius, saliva, and facial movement; a distal lesion beyond stylomastoid foramen primarily affects motor branches. The combination localizes the lesion.
cn-31: Five major terminal VII branch groups: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical; branches overlap and form variable connections.

Temporal/zygomatic branches supply upper facial regions including brow/eyelid movement; buccal branches supply midface/buccinator/oral muscles; marginal mandibular supplies lower-lip muscles; cervical supplies platysma.
In the original diagram, the branches radiate through/after parotid gland across the face; selective branch injury can cause regional weakness rather than an entire peripheral facial palsy.
cn-32: Orbital group: orbicularis oculi closes eyelids; corrugator supercilii draws the medial eyebrow down/in during frowning. The slide's 'Orbital oculi' is a typographic form of orbicularis oculi.
Nasal group: procerus wrinkles the nasal bridge; nasalis compresses or dilates nasal aperture through its parts; depressor septi nasi helps move the nasal septum/ala inferiorly.
Oral sphincter/cheek: orbicularis oris closes/protrudes lips; buccinator presses the cheek against teeth to keep food on occlusal surfaces. Buccinator is VII motor despite its role during eating.

Elevators: levator labii superioris alaeque nasi raises upper lip/ala; levator labii superioris and zygomaticus minor raise upper lip; zygomaticus major raises mouth corner; levator anguli oris raises oral angle; risorius retracts the angle laterally.
Depressors/chin: depressor anguli oris lowers mouth corner; depressor labii inferioris lowers lower lip; mentalis elevates/protrudes lower lip and wrinkles chin.

Other VII muscles: platysma tenses neck skin and helps lower mouth/mandible; auricular muscles move pinna; occipitofrontalis moves scalp and raises eyebrows through its frontal belly. All named facial-expression groups are branchial motor rather than trigeminal mastication muscles.
cn-33: Most cranial motor nuclei receive bilateral corticobulbar input; lower facial motor pools and genioglossus receive predominantly contralateral drive.
A unilateral supranuclear/UMN lesion classically weakens contralateral lower face with relative forehead sparing because upper-face input is more bilateral.

A facial nucleus/fascicle or peripheral VII lesion produces ipsilateral upper and lower facial weakness, including brow elevation and eye closure. An LMN pattern can therefore occur from a pontine lesion, not only a peripheral nerve lesion.
Bell palsy is an idiopathic peripheral VII palsy, a diagnosis requiring an appropriate clinical pattern; forehead involvement alone does not identify its cause.
Forehead sparing is a useful tendency rather than an absolute rule in every central facial lesion.
cn-34: Corneal touch travels through nasociliary V1 afferents into trigeminal sensory circuits; bilateral interneuronal connections activate facial motor output.
VII activates orbicularis oculi to close each eyelid; normal stimulation of either cornea causes bilateral blink. V1 in → VII out.
Unilateral V1 afferent damage: stimulating that cornea fails to trigger either blink, but stimulating the intact cornea can trigger both if VII outputs are intact.
Unilateral VII efferent damage: the affected eye does not close regardless of which cornea is stimulated, while the intact eye can blink to either stimulus.
cn-36: CN VIII is SSA for hearing and vestibular sensation and attaches near the lateral pontomedullary junction.
It shares internal acoustic meatus with VII; cochlear and vestibular sensory nuclei span the pontomedullary region rather than fitting a single sharply bounded level.
Cochlear input arises from auditory hair-cell circuits and spiral ganglion neurons; vestibular input arises from semicircular/otolith circuits through vestibular ganglion neurons.
The original inner-ear diagram labels cochlea, vestibule/semicircular structures, and facial/vestibulocochlear routes for visual identification.
cn-37: Cochlear division conveys hearing from cochlea to cochlear nuclei; peripheral injury can cause ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus.
Vestibular division conveys head-motion/orientation information to vestibular nuclei; lesions can cause vertigo, nystagmus, and imbalance.

Semicircular canals principally sense angular acceleration; utricle/saccule sense linear acceleration and gravitational tilt. Vestibular function also coordinates gaze through vestibulo-ocular circuits.
Central auditory pathways become substantially bilateral above cochlear nuclei, so one central lesion often causes less complete unilateral deafness than one peripheral VIII lesion.
cn-38: Vestibular schwannoma is a Schwann-cell tumor usually arising from the vestibular division of VIII, often beginning in internal acoustic meatus and extending into CPA.
Unilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance are common presentations. 'Acoustic neuroma' is a historical term that misstates both the usual division and cell type.
Large tumors can compress VII causing facial weakness and V causing face sensory/corneal reflex deficits; cerebellar/brainstem compression can add ataxia or other findings.
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas strongly suggest an NF2-related tumor-predisposition syndrome; do not infer this from every solitary unilateral tumor.
cn-39: Ménière disease is associated with endolymphatic hydrops/distention in the membranous labyrinth, affecting cochlear and vestibular function; its complete cause is not explained by pressure alone.
Classic pattern: recurrent spontaneous vertigo, tinnitus, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and aural fullness, often unilateral early.
Stress, fatigue, illness, or dietary factors may be reported triggers, but are not independently diagnostic.
Differentiate episodic inner-ear symptoms from progressive vestibular schwannoma and brief position-triggered vertigo such as BPPV; the symptom time course matters.
cn-41: IX emerges from medulla and exits through jugular foramen. SVE supplies stylopharyngeus for pharyngeal elevation/swallowing; GVE supplies parotid secretomotor pathway.
SVA carries posterior one-third tongue taste; GVA carries carotid sinus stretch and carotid body chemistry; the slide categorizes posterior tongue/oropharynx/middle-ear general sensation as GSA.
Somatic versus visceral classification of some mucosal afferents varies by convention; preserve the clinically useful territories and distinguish taste from general sensation.
Parotid route: inferior salivatory nucleus → IX/tympanic branch and plexus → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal V3 hitchhiking → parotid.
IX provides the classic afferent limb of the gag reflex; it does not supply most pharyngeal/laryngeal motor muscles.
cn-42: X emerges from medulla and exits jugular foramen. SVE supplies most palate/pharynx/larynx muscles; exceptions include stylopharyngeus IX and tensor veli palatini V3.
GVE supplies parasympathetic thoracic and abdominal viscera, classically through foregut/midgut; pelvic splanchnics supply hindgut and pelvic organs.

SVA includes taste near epiglottis/most posterior tongue; visceral afferents convey thoracoabdominal information. Small external-ear and mucosal sensory territories are also carried by X, with GSA/GVA naming varying by region/convention.
The original distribution image traces vagal branches through thorax into abdominal plexuses and relates recurrent laryngeal branches to the great arteries.
cn-43: Nucleus ambiguus supplies branchial motor output through IX/X to pharyngeal/laryngeal structures; stylopharyngeus is the IX motor example.

Inferior salivatory GVE neurons → IX → parotid route. Dorsal motor X supplies much vagal preganglionic output to thoracoabdominal organs; cardiac vagal neurons also include ambiguus-related populations.
Solitary nucleus handles rostral taste and caudal visceral input through VII/IX/X; spinal trigeminal nucleus handles general somatic input from V and small VII/IX/X territories.
Sensory input and motor output can share a nerve while terminating/originating in different nuclei; a whole-nerve lesion can therefore affect several functional components.
cn-44: Vagal motor weakness can cause dysphagia, hoarseness, impaired pharyngeal contraction, and ipsilateral palatal droop.
On phonation, the intact side pulls the uvula away from the weak side; e.g., left X weakness → left palatal droop and uvula toward the right.
A proximal X lesion can affect both palate and larynx; an isolated recurrent laryngeal lesion can cause hoarseness while sparing the palate.
An absent gag is not alone diagnostic because normal variation and technique matter; combine it with voice, swallowing, palate, and associated signs.
cn-45: Classic gag circuit: touch posterior pharynx → IX afferent → medullary interneurons → X efferent/ambiguus motor → bilateral pharyngeal contraction/elevation.
IX in → X out is the standard board-style pairing; actual oral/pharyngeal reflex sensory inputs can include other nerves depending on the stimulated site.
Testing sides can separate sensory input failure from motor response failure, but gag variability means absence alone is less informative than a coherent bulbar examination.
cn-46: Superior laryngeal external branch supplies cricothyroid, which tensions vocal folds for pitch; internal branch supplies sensation above vocal folds and enters near the thyrohyoid membrane.
Recurrent/inferior laryngeal supplies intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid and sensation below folds. Posterior cricoarytenoid is the principal vocal-fold abductor.
Right recurrent laryngeal loops under right subclavian artery; left loops under aortic arch near ligamentum arteriosum, then both ascend toward larynx.
Important abbreviation clarification: 'right SCA' in this slide means subclavian artery, not the superior cerebellar artery used elsewhere in the deck.
Thyroid/neck surgery can injure laryngeal nerves. External-branch injury impairs pitch; unilateral RLN injury can cause hoarseness; bilateral abductor dysfunction can threaten airway.
cn-48: Spinal accessory motor neurons arise in upper cervical cord, roughly C1-C5; rootlets ascend through foramen magnum and leave skull through jugular foramen.
XI supplies ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. SCM rotates the face to the opposite side; trapezius elevates/stabilizes the shoulder girdle.
The traditional 'cranial accessory' component is commonly treated functionally with vagus; distinguish it from spinal XI supplying SCM/trapezius.
cn-49: Unilateral XI injury weakens ipsilateral shoulder shrug/trapezius and can produce shoulder droop.
Ipsilateral SCM weakness makes it difficult to turn the face away from the lesion against resistance: right XI injury → weak right shrug and weak head turn left.
Posterior-triangle neck procedures can injure XI; compare shoulder elevation and resisted head rotation rather than interpreting head posture alone.
cn-50: Hypoglossal GSE nucleus is in medulla; XII rootlets emerge between pyramid and olive and exit skull through hypoglossal canal.
XII supplies intrinsic tongue muscles plus genioglossus, hyoglossus, and styloglossus; palatoglossus is the CN X exception.
Genioglossus protrudes the tongue, and unequal force determines deviation. C1 fibers can hitchhike with XII to geniohyoid/thyrohyoid but are not hypoglossal-origin motor fibers.
cn-51: Peripheral/nuclear XII LMN injury produces ipsilateral tongue weakness, wasting, and fasciculations; on protrusion the tongue points toward the weak side/lesion.
A unilateral supranuclear lesion classically weakens contralateral genioglossus without prominent denervation atrophy, so protrusion points away from the cortical lesion.
Example: right XII nerve injury → rightward tongue with right wasting; right corticobulbar injury → leftward tongue with left genioglossus weakness.
The constant rule is 'toward the weak genioglossus'; relating that to lesion side depends on whether the lesion is above or below the corticobulbar connection.
cn-52: Anterior two-thirds tongue general sensation travels in lingual V3; taste travels in chorda tympani VII after joining lingual nerve.
Posterior one-third general sensation and taste travel in IX; epiglottic/most posterior tongue regions include X.
Circumvallate papillae are a useful exception: they lie near the anterior/posterior boundary but are typically supplied for taste by IX.
Tongue motor is XII except palatoglossus X. Sensory/taste and motor are separate modalities, so one lesion can spare one while impairing another.
cn-54: Corticospinal carries descending voluntary motor commands; medial lemniscus carries body fine touch/vibration/position after dorsal-column relay; spinothalamic carries body pain/temperature.
The figure traces first-, second-, and third-order sensory neurons and motor neuron chains across spinal cord, brainstem, thalamus, and cortex.
Determine whether the damaged fibers have crossed before predicting deficit side; a pathway name alone is insufficient without lesion level.
cn-55: Corticospinal fibers cross at pyramidal decussation in caudal medulla; a typical brainstem lesion above that crossing causes contralateral limb weakness.

Dorsal-column sensory axons relay in gracile/cuneate nuclei, then internal arcuate fibers cross in caudal medulla to form medial lemniscus. Above crossing, injury produces contralateral vibration/position loss.
Spinothalamic fibers crossed near spinal entry and ascend contralaterally through brainstem; brainstem injury therefore causes contralateral body pain-temperature loss.
At a decussation or in a complex lesion, findings may not fit a simple single-side rule; the standard patterns assume one tract segment on one side.
cn-56: Face touch/vibration relays mainly in principal V nucleus; face pain/temperature uses spinal V tract/nucleus. Body equivalents are medial lemniscus and spinothalamic pathways.
A lateral brainstem lesion can interrupt ipsilateral face pain fibers before crossing and contralateral body pain fibers after crossing, producing crossed sensory loss.
Somatosensory face input chiefly relays to VPM thalamus; body input chiefly to VPL. A cranial sensory deficit plus opposite body deficit is a strong brainstem localization clue.
cn-57: This image-only chart is transcribed here: GSE column → oculomotor III and trochlear IV in midbrain, abducens VI in pons, hypoglossal XII in medulla.
Branchial motor/SVE column → motor V in pons, facial VII in pons, ambiguus for IX/X in medulla, and spinal accessory nucleus in upper cervical cord.
The chart also labels XI with ambiguus using traditional cranial-accessory terminology; those cranial fibers are generally considered functionally vagal, distinct from spinal XI to SCM/trapezius.
GVE column → Edinger-Westphal III in midbrain, superior salivatory VII in pons, inferior salivatory IX and dorsal motor X in medulla.
SVA/GVA column → solitary nucleus receiving VII/IX/X, with taste mainly rostral and visceral input mainly caudal.
GSA column → mesencephalic V for proprioception, principal V for discriminative touch, spinal V tract/nucleus for pain-temperature/crude somatic input including small VII/IX/X contributions.
SSA column → vestibular/cochlear VIII nuclei at pontomedullary levels. Vision and smell are special afferent modalities but their primary structures are not part of this brainstem nuclei chart.

Motor is shown medial to sulcus limitans and sensory lateral; vertical boundaries mark midbrain, pons, medulla, and extension into cord. These are schematic functional columns rather than a literal axial image.
cn-58: Read a section systematically: identify level → use aqueduct/fourth ventricle/colliculi/olive/pyramids for orientation → identify CN nuclei/fascicles → find corticospinal/medial lemniscus/spinothalamic → distinguish medial/lateral.

The central medulla image locates XII/dorsal motor X and solitary structures near fourth ventricular floor, pyramids ventrally, inferior olives ventrolaterally, and inferior cerebellar peduncles dorsolaterally.

A nucleus is a collection of neuronal somata; a fascicle is axons traveling inside brainstem toward a nerve root. Nearby long tracts can add contralateral limb signs to an ipsilateral cranial deficit.
cn-59: Rostral midbrain: superior colliculus dorsally, cerebral aqueduct surrounded by periaqueductal gray, and oculomotor/EW structures near the midline tegmentum.
Crus cerebri contains corticospinal/corticobulbar and corticopontine fibers ventrally; substantia nigra separates ventral basis from tegmental structures.
Red nucleus lies in tegmentum; medial lemniscus and anterolateral/spinothalamic pathways traverse more lateral sensory regions.
The labeled section also shows MLF, mesencephalic V, oculomotor fascicles, and central tegmental fibers. Superior colliculus + III is the level-identification pair.
cn-60: Caudal midbrain: inferior colliculus auditory structure, aqueduct/periaqueductal gray, trochlear nucleus, and IV fibers heading dorsally to cross/exit.
Superior cerebellar peduncle decussation is a key tegmental landmark; substantia nigra and ventral crus cerebri remain visible.
The diagram labels MLF, mesencephalic V, lateral/medial lemniscal and spinothalamic regions, and descending motor fibers. Inferior colliculus + IV identifies caudal midbrain.
Sensory DCML crossing is in medulla, whereas the prominent crossing at this midbrain level is superior cerebellar peduncle; do not confuse the two.
cn-61: Rostral pons has a large basis pontis and middle cerebellar peduncles; mesencephalic V extends into this region.
Pontine nuclei and transverse pontine fibers connect cerebral input to cerebellum, mainly through the opposite middle cerebellar peduncle.
Descending corticospinal/corticobulbar bundles run through basis; medial lemniscus and other sensory tracts are more dorsal/tegmental.
The original image also labels trigeminal lemniscus, MLF, superior cerebellar peduncle, and tectospinal-related region. Large basis + middle peduncle is the gross pons clue.
cn-62: Middle pons: principal sensory and motor V nuclei are key identifiers adjacent to trigeminal root pathways; fourth ventricle is dorsal and middle cerebellar peduncle lateral.
Basis contains pontine nuclei, transverse pontocerebellar fibers, and descending corticospinal/corticobulbar bundles.
Medial lemniscus, MLF, and other sensory/long tracts traverse tegmentum. MLF coordinates ocular motor nuclei and vestibular gaze signals.
The labeled plate also identifies spinothalamic and lateral-lemniscal regions; CN V nuclei are the major level-localization feature.
cn-63: Caudal pons: facial colliculus is formed by VII fibers looping around VI nucleus near fourth ventricular floor; it is not simply the facial motor nucleus.
Abducens, facial, vestibular, and spinal trigeminal structures coexist with corticospinal and medial lemniscal pathways.
Middle and inferior cerebellar peduncles connect the adjacent cerebellar/vestibular circuitry; the plate also labels MLF, superior olive, trapezoid-body/auditory regions, and spinothalamic pathways.
VI/VII signs plus a facial colliculus lesion localize to caudal pons; a whole VI nucleus lesion can cause ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy.
cn-64: Open/upper medulla borders fourth ventricle and contains a prominent inferior olive; ventral pyramid carries corticospinal fibers.
Dorsolateral structures include vestibular nuclei, solitary nucleus/tract, spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract, and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
The full labeled section also shows XII and dorsal motor X near ventricular floor, ambiguus deeper laterally, medial lemniscus, spinothalamic regions, and MLF.
Inferior olive + open fourth ventricle identifies rostral medulla; dorsal motor X and XII structures help distinguish its nuclei from pontine VI/VII.
cn-65: Central medulla nuclear map: XII and dorsal motor X are dorsomedial; solitary is more lateral; ambiguus lies deeper in lateral tegmentum; spinal V nucleus/tract is lateral.
Medial group for localization: XII fibers/nucleus, pyramid/corticospinal, medial lemniscus. Lateral group: ambiguus, spinal V, spinothalamic, vestibular/cerebellar connections.
Inferior olive is ventrolateral; inferior cerebellar peduncle is dorsolateral; fourth ventricle is dorsal. MLF and reticular regions lie in the tegmental network.
This layout predicts medial motor/position patterns versus lateral bulbar/crossed pain-temperature/ataxia patterns.
cn-66: Closed caudal medulla has a central canal rather than an open ventricular floor; gracile/cuneate nuclei receive ipsilateral dorsal-column input.
Internal arcuate fibers cross to form medial lemniscus at the sensory decussation; corticospinal fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation farther caudally.
The figure shows these at adjacent levels, not one obligatory identical plane for both crossings. Pyramids occupy the ventral medulla before fibers enter lateral cord.
Spinal trigeminal and spinothalamic pathways remain in lateral regions; gracile is medial/lower-body and cuneate lateral/upper-body.
cn-67: Review vascular map: PCA/SCA branches → midbrain; basilar pontine branches with AICA/SCA contributions → pons; vertebral/PICA/ASA branches → medulla.

A medial medullary pattern can combine ipsilateral XII LMN signs with contralateral motor and vibration-position deficits; a lateral medullary pattern favors crossed pain-temperature, bulbar signs, vertigo, and ataxia.

These are related board-review applications of the anatomy; the deck defers detailed vascular syndromes to a later lecture. Vessel territories vary, so localize from structures rather than a mnemonic alone.
